We use the future continuous to talk about actions that will be happening during a period of time in the future.

We can use the future continuous in different situations:

1. When projecting ourselves into the future.
Example:
This afternoon, we will be evaluating our metrics.

2. When predicting something that can happen in the future.
Example:
Next month, our manager is going to be evaluating the performance of the project.

3. When talking about continuous events that will take place in the future.
Example:
When we test the code, we will be evaluating the code coverage metric.

The structure of the future continuous is as follows:

We use the future perfect to refer to an action that will have finished at a point in the future.

Although this tense is not too common, we can use it when we want to talk about an action that will take place in the future but that will be finished before the event we are mentioning takes place.

Example: By next month, we will have finished the project.

We can also use this tense when we want to clarify that an action in the future occurs before another action.

Example: Before we use code coverage as a metric, we will have determined what testing parameters to use.

Take a look at the previous examples. Notice that when we have the future perfect tense, we specify the moment or event that takes place after the action of the future perfect. This moment or event is usually introduced by the preposition ‘by' or by the action that will take place afterwards.

Monica: I'm going to be writing the code for a new application. I'm still figuring out how coding works, and I want to clear up some doubts first. I'm aware that many developers love using the code coverage metric, but I think it's overrated.
Jonathan:It's good to be critical with the metrics you're using. From what I can tell you, once we have tested the code, the code coverage is going to let you know where and how much of the code remains untested. You're then going to be deciding whether it's worth testing the remaining code. This depends on how your application works. Likewise, if you're writing getters and setters, you're not going to be having to test them nor the code because that'll be generating automatically.

Monica: So, by the time I prove that the application is working fine, I'll have finished everything, and I won't be needing any further testing, right?
Jonathan: Most likely not. You'll be needing more tests if there's an important malfunction in the application. On the other hand, we cannot trust the code coverage metric when it comes to the assessment of the quality of the tested code. The metric will only tell you how much of the code you'll have tested but not how good the testing was. Therefore, you'll be exercising caution when interpreting the results of the code coverage metric.

Monica: Alright, this metric won't be assessing the quality of tests, but showing which lines of the code were untested. However, as I'm following a test-driven development method, I'm supposed to have a high percentage of covered code unlike other methods where testing is not at the core of the development process, am I right?
Jonathan:Exactly, by the time you get to 80% of code coverage, you'll have tested the necessary.
